title: Theorem

label: question:WZ-symmetric
title: Question
body_md:
\label{question:WZ-symmetric}
Does the Loss--Yau potential minimize $J_2$ in the invariant class $Y^G$?
Equivalently,
\[
 J_2(A_{\mathrm{LY}})
 \stackrel{?}{=}
 \inf_{A\in Y^G}J_2(A).
\]
head: environment
name: Wang--Zhang, dimension three

label: lem:gauge
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Consider the convex differentiable functional
\[
 F(\phi):=\frac1q\lVert A-\nabla\phi\rVert_{q}^q,
 \qquad \phi\in\dot W^{1,q}(\mathbb{R}^n).
\]
Since $\lvert A\rvert^{q-2}A\in L^{q/(q-1)}$, the distributional condition
\eqref{eq:nonlinear-gauge-q}, H\"older's inequality, and the standard
density of $C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ in $\dot W^{1,q}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ with respect to
the gradient norm imply
\[
 F'(0)[\phi]
 =-\int_{\mathbb{R}^n}\lvert A\rvert^{q-2}A\cdot\nabla\phi\,\mathrm{d} x=0
 \qquad\text{for every }\phi\in\dot W^{1,q}(\mathbb{R}^n).
\]
Convexity now gives
\[
 F(\phi)\geq F(0)+F'(0)[\phi]=F(0).
\]
Thus the infimum is attained at $\phi=0$, which proves the assertion.
head: environment

title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The Pauli relations give
\[
 (\boldsymbol{\sigma}\cdot a)^2=\lvert a\rvert^2I_{\mathbb{C}^2},
 \qquad a\in\mathbb{R}^3.
\]
Therefore
\[
 \lvert \boldsymbol{\sigma}\cdot(-i\nabla)(u\eta)\rvert^2
 =\langle \eta,(\boldsymbol{\sigma}\cdot\nabla u)^2\eta\rangle
 =\lvert \nabla u\rvert^2\lvert \eta\rvert^2.
\]
head: environment

label: thm:FL-spinor-all-d
title: Theorem
head: environment

label: eq:radial-integration-d
title: Proof
body_md:
For a real-valued weakly differentiable function $v$ and a constant unit
spinor $\eta$, the Clifford relations give
\[
 \lvert D_d(v\eta)\rvert^2
 =\langle \eta,(\boldsymbol{\gamma}\cdot\nabla v)^2\eta\rangle
 =\lvert \nabla v\rvert^2.
\]
For the function in \eqref{eq:AT-spinor-d},
\[
 u_d^{q_d}=(1+r^{q_d})^{-d},
 \qquad
 \lvert u_d'(r)\rvert
 =d r^{q_d-1}(1+r^{q_d})^{-(d+1)/2}.
\]
For every radial integrand $F$, polar coordinates mean
\begin{equation}\label{eq:radial-integration-d}
 \int_{\mathbb{R}^d}F(\lvert x\rvert)\,\mathrm{d} x
 =\lvert \mathbb{S}^{d-1}\rvert\int_0^\infty F(r)r^{d-1}\,\mathrm{d} r.
\end{equation}
In the first integral below, set $t=r^{q_d}$. Since
$r^{d-1}\,\mathrm{d} r=q_d^{-1}t^{d/q_d-1}\,\mathrm{d} t$ and
$d/q_d=(d-1)/2$, \eqref{eq:beta-infinite-interval} gives
\begin{align*}
 \int_{\mathbb{R}^d}u_d^{q_d}\,\mathrm{d} x
 &=\frac{\lvert \mathbb{S}^{d-1}\rvert}{q_d}
   \int_0^\infty
   \frac{t^{(d-1)/2-1}}{(1+t)^d}\,\mathrm{d} t=\frac{\lvert \mathbb{S}^{d-1}\rvert}{q_d}
   \mathrm B\left(\frac{d-1}{2},\frac{d+1}{2}\right)
   =I_d^{\mathrm{AT}},\\
 \int_{\mathbb{R}^d}\lvert \nabla u_d\rvert^{p_d}\,\mathrm{d} x
 &=\frac{d^{p_d}\lvert \mathbb{S}^{d-1}\rvert}{q_d}
   \int_0^\infty
   \frac{t^{(d+1)/2-1}}{(1+t)^d}\,\mathrm{d} t=\frac{d^{p_d}\lvert \mathbb{S}^{d-1}\rvert}{q_d}
   \mathrm B\left(\frac{d+1}{2},\frac{d-1}{2}\right)
   =d^{p_d}I_d^{\mathrm{AT}}.
\end{align*}
For the second computation we used
$p_d(q_d-1)=q_d$ and $p_d(d+1)/2=d$. 
Since $1-p_d/q_d=2/(d+1)$, this proves
\eqref{eq:AT-quotient-d}.

For comparison, we compute the known quotient of the Frank--Loss family
in our normalization; see \cite[Appendix~C]{WangZhangSpinor}.
The identities \eqref{eq:Clifford-relations} and
\eqref{eq:FL-family-conditions-d} imply
\begin{align*}
 \lvert \phi_0+\boldsymbol{\gamma}\cdot x\phi_1\rvert^2
 &=a^2(1+\lvert x\rvert^2),\\
 \lvert \boldsymbol{\gamma}\cdot x\phi_0-\phi_1\rvert^2
 &=a^2(1+\lvert x\rvert^2).
\end{align*}
Consequently,
\begin{equation*}
 \lvert \Psi_{\phi_0,\phi_1}(x)\rvert
 =a(1+\lvert x\rvert^2)^{-(d-1)/2}.
\end{equation*}
A direct differentiation gives
\begin{equation*}
 D_d\Psi_{\phi_0,\phi_1}
 =i d(1+\lvert x\rvert^2)^{-(d+2)/2}
   (\boldsymbol{\gamma}\cdot x\phi_0-\phi_1),
\end{equation*}
and hence
\begin{equation*}
 \lvert D_d\Psi_{\phi_0,\phi_1}(x)\rvert
 =da(1+\lvert x\rvert^2)^{-(d+1)/2}.
\end{equation*}
Using \eqref{eq:radial-integration-d} and the substitution $t=|x|^2$, we have
\begin{align*}
 \int_{\mathbb{R}^d}(1+\lvert x\rvert^2)^{-d}\,\mathrm{d} x
 =\frac{\lvert \mathbb{S}^{d-1}\rvert}{2}
   \int_0^\infty\frac{t^{d/2-1}}{(1+t)^d}\,\mathrm{d} t
 =\frac{\lvert \mathbb{S}^{d-1}\rvert}{2}\mathrm B\left(\frac d2,\frac d2\right)
 =I_d^{\mathrm{FL}}.
\end{align*}
The first closed form in \eqref{eq:I-FL-d} follows from
\eqref{eq:gamma-beta-definitions} and \eqref{eq:sphere-area}. The second one
follows from Legendre's duplication formula
\begin{equation}\label{eq:gamma-duplication}
 \Gamma(z)\Gamma(z+\tfrac12)
 =2^{1-2z}\sqrt\pi\,\Gamma(2z).
\end{equation}
Indeed, applying it with $z=d/2$ gives
$\pi^{d/2}\Gamma(d/2)/\Gamma(d)=\lvert \mathbb{S}^d\rvert/2^d$.
Consequently,
\[
 \int_{\mathbb{R}^d}\lvert \Psi_{\phi_0,\phi_1}\rvert^{q_d}\,\mathrm{d} x
 =a^{q_d}I_d^{\mathrm{FL}},
 \qquad
 \int_{\mathbb{R}^d}\lvert D_d\Psi_{\phi_0,\phi_1}\rvert^{p_d}\,\mathrm{d} x
 =d^{p_d}a^{p_d}I_d^{\mathrm{FL}}.
\]
This proves \eqref{eq:FL-quotient-d}.

For completeness, the equality in \eqref{eq:integral-ratio-d} follows by
writing both beta functions in gamma form:
\begin{align*}
 \frac{I_d^{\mathrm{AT}}}{I_d^{\mathrm{FL}}}
 =\frac{2}{q_d}
   \frac{\Gamma((d-1)/2)\Gamma((d+1)/2)}{\Gamma(d/2)^2}=\frac{(d-1)^2}{2d}
   \left(\frac{\Gamma((d-1)/2)}{\Gamma(d/2)}\right)^2.
\end{align*}
Here we used $2/q_d=(d-1)/d$ and
$\Gamma((d+1)/2)=((d-1)/2)\Gamma((d-1)/2)$.
To prove strictness, put
$x=(d-1)/2>0$. Strict log-convexity of the gamma function, applied at the
midpoint $x+1$ of $x+1/2$ and $x+3/2$, gives
\[
 \Gamma(x+1)^2
 <\Gamma(x+1/2)\Gamma(x+3/2)
 =(x+1/2)\Gamma(x+1/2)^2.
\]
Since $\Gamma(x+1)=x\Gamma(x)$, it follows that
\[
 \frac{\Gamma(x+1/2)}{\Gamma(x)}
 >\frac{x}{\sqrt{x+1/2}}.
\]
Indeed,
\[
 \frac{I_d^{\mathrm{AT}}}{I_d^{\mathrm{FL}}}
 =\frac{x^2}{x+1/2}
  \left(\frac{\Gamma(x)}{\Gamma(x+1/2)}\right)^2<1,
\]
which is the strict inequality in \eqref{eq:integral-ratio-d}. Both trial
families belong to the natural
spaces in \eqref{eq:FL-sharp-spinor-general}.
The conclusion \eqref{eq:FL-disproof-d} follows.
head: environment

title: Corollary
body_md:
For $d=3$, one has
\[
 I_3^{\mathrm{AT}}=\frac{2\pi}{3},
 \qquad I_3^{\mathrm{FL}}=\frac{\pi^2}{4},
\]
and therefore
\begin{equation*}
 S_3^s
 \leq\sqrt{18\pi}
 <\frac{3\sqrt3}{2}\pi.
\end{equation*}

label: lem:vector-conformal-invariance
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:vector-conformal-invariance}
Let $d\geq3$ and let $F$ be a M\"obius transformation of
$\mathbb{R}^d\cup\{\infty\}$. Identifying vector fields with one-forms, define
\[
 (F^*A)(x):=DF(x)^T A(F(x))
\]
away from the possible pole of $F$. Then $F^*$ maps $Y_d$ bijectively
onto itself and preserves both $\lVert \nabla\wedge A\rVert_{L^{d/2}}$ and
$\VERT A\VERT_{d}$. In particular, it preserves $R_d^v$ and $\mathcal Q_d^v$
whenever $\nabla\wedge A\neq0$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Write $DF=\lambda O$, with $O$ orthogonal and $\lambda>0$.
Pullback multiplies the pointwise norm of a $k$-form by $\lambda^k$,
whereas $\lvert \det DF\rvert=\lambda^d$. Change of variables therefore
preserves the $L^d$ norm of one-forms and the $L^{d/2}$ norm of two-forms.
Exterior differentiation commutes with pullback away from the pole.
The identity extends distributionally across the pole: with balls
centred there and a cutoff supported in $B_{2\varepsilon}$, equal to
one on $B_\varepsilon$, and satisfying
$\lvert \nabla\chi_\varepsilon\rvert\leq C/\varepsilon$, the additional term
against any fixed smooth test form is bounded by
\[
 C\lVert F^*A\rVert_{L^d(B_{2\varepsilon})}
   \lVert \nabla\chi_\varepsilon\rVert_{L^{d/(d-1)}}
 \leq C\varepsilon^{d-2}
   \lVert F^*A\rVert_{L^d(B_{2\varepsilon})}\longrightarrow0.
\]
Thus a pulled-back $L^d$ gradient remains distributionally closed on
$\mathbb{R}^d$. The distributional Poincar\'e lemma makes it a gradient of a
function in $\dot W^{1,d}(\mathbb{R}^d)$. Applying the same argument to $F^{-1}$
shows that pullback maps the gradient subspace onto itself.
Its $L^d$ isometry consequently preserves distance to that subspace,
which is precisely $\VERT A\VERT_{d}$.

label: thm:FL-vector-all-d
title: Theorem
head: environment

label: eq:vector-trial-nonlinear-d
title: Proof
body_md:
Write $v=(-x_2,x_1,0,\ldots,0)$. Since
\begin{equation}\label{eq:vector-trial-nonlinear-d}
 \lvert A_{\mathcal{T},d}\rvert^{d-2}A_{\mathcal{T},d}
 =d^{d-1}\rho^{d-2}s^{-2(d-1)}v,
\end{equation}
the divergence vanishes away from the axis $\{\rho=0\}$: the scalar
coefficient is constant along planar rotations, while
$\nabla\cdot v=0$. The Cartesian field on the right-hand side of
\eqref{eq:vector-trial-nonlinear-d} is locally $W^{1,1}$ across the axis
for $d\geq3$, so the identity also holds distributionally.
Since $A_{\mathcal{T},d}(x)=O(\lvert x\rvert^{-3})$ and
$\nabla\wedge A_{\mathcal{T},d}(x)=O(\lvert x\rvert^{-4})$ as $\lvert x\rvert\to\infty$,
the field belongs to $Y_d$.
Lemma~\ref{lem:gauge}, with $n=q=d$, proves
\eqref{eq:vector-trial-gauge-d}.

For $j\geq3$, direct differentiation gives
\begin{align*}
 F_{12}&=2d\,s^{-3}(s-2\rho^2),\\
 F_{1j}&=-4d\,x_2x_j s^{-3},
 \qquad
 F_{2j}=4d\,x_1x_j s^{-3},
\end{align*}
where throughout this proof
$F_{ij}:=\partial_i(A_{\mathcal{T},d})_j-\partial_j(A_{\mathcal{T},d})_i$.
Writing $z=(x_3,\ldots,x_d)$, we obtain
\begin{align}
 \lvert \nabla\wedge A_{\mathcal{T},d}\rvert^2
 &=(2d)^2s^{-6}\bigl((s-2\rho^2)^2+4\rho^2\lvert z\rvert^2\bigr)=(2d)^2s^{-6}(s^2-4\rho^2).
 \label{eq:vector-trial-pointwise-d}
\end{align}

Let $\Phi:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{S}^d\setminus\{(0,\ldots,0,-1)\}$ be inverse
stereographic projection. In coordinates,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:stereographic-T-d}
\begin{aligned}
 y_j&=\frac{2x_j}{s}\quad(1\leq j\leq d),
 & y_{d+1}&=\frac{1-\lvert x\rvert^2}{s},\\
 \,\mathrm{d}\omega_{\mathbb{S}^d}&=2^ds^{-d}\,\mathrm{d} x,
 & T:=y_1^2+y_2^2&=\frac{4\rho^2}{s^2},
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
where $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$ and $y \in \mathbb{S}^d\setminus\{(0,\ldots,0,-1)\}$. The measure identity is understood under the change of variables
$y=\Phi(x)$. The Jacobian factor $2^ds^{-d}$ follows directly from the derivative matrix
of $\Phi$ (equivalently, from the fact that every tangent length is
multiplied by $2/s$).
Moreover,
$A_{\mathcal{T},d}^\flat=(d/4)\Phi^*(y_1\,\mathrm{d} y_2-y_2\,\mathrm{d} y_1)$,
so the trial potential comes from a multiple of the one-form dual to
the standard rotation field in the $(y_1,y_2)$-plane of $\mathbb{S}^d$.

For every integrable function $h:[0,1]\to\mathbb{R}$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:spherical-slicing-d}
 \int_{\mathbb{S}^d}h(y_1^2+y_2^2)\,\mathrm{d}\omega_{\mathbb{S}^d}
 =\frac{d-1}{2}\lvert \mathbb{S}^d\rvert
   \int_0^1 h(t)(1-t)^{(d-3)/2}\,\mathrm{d} t.
\end{equation}
Indeed, outside a set of surface measure zero we may parameterize $\mathbb{S}^d$
by
\[
 y=\bigl(\sqrt t\cos\theta,\sqrt t\sin\theta,
          \sqrt{1-t}\,\omega\bigr),
 \quad 0<t<1,\quad 0\leq\theta<2\pi,
 \quad \omega\in\mathbb{S}^{d-2}.
\]
The coordinate vectors in the $t$, $\theta$, and $\omega$ directions are
orthogonal, and the induced surface Jacobian is
\[
 \frac12(1-t)^{(d-3)/2}.
\]
Therefore
\[
 \int_{\mathbb{S}^d}h(y_1^2+y_2^2)\,\mathrm{d}\omega_{\mathbb{S}^d}
 =\pi\lvert \mathbb{S}^{d-2}\rvert
  \int_0^1h(t)(1-t)^{(d-3)/2}\,\mathrm{d} t.
\]
Since
$\pi\lvert \mathbb{S}^{d-2}\rvert=\frac{d-1}{2}\lvert \mathbb{S}^d\rvert$,
formula \eqref{eq:spherical-slicing-d} follows.

Applying \eqref{eq:spherical-slicing-d} first with $h(t)=t^{d/2}$ and
then with $h(t)=(1-t)^{d/4}$ gives, purely by one-dimensional integration,
\begin{align}
 \frac1{\lvert \mathbb{S}^d\rvert}\int_{\mathbb{S}^d}T^{d/2}\,\mathrm{d}\omega_{\mathbb{S}^d}
 &=\frac{d-1}{2}
   \mathrm B\left(1+\frac d2,\frac{d-1}{2}\right)=\frac{\Gamma(1+d/2)\Gamma((d+1)/2)}{\Gamma(d+1/2)}
 =G_d,
 \notag \\
 \frac1{\lvert \mathbb{S}^d\rvert}\int_{\mathbb{S}^d}(1-T)^{d/4}\,\mathrm{d}\omega_{\mathbb{S}^d}
 &=\frac{d-1}{2}
   \int_0^1(1-t)^{(d-3)/2+d/4}\,\mathrm{d} t=\frac{2(d-1)}{3d-2}=b_d.
 \label{eq:one-minus-T-integral-d}
\end{align}

Finally, \eqref{eq:gamma-duplication} with $z=(d+1)/2$ gives
\[
 \Gamma(1+d/2)\Gamma((d+1)/2)
 =2^{-d}\sqrt\pi\,\Gamma(d+1).
\]
The same formula with $z=d+1/2$ reads
$\Gamma(d+1/2)\Gamma(d+1)=2^{-2d}\sqrt\pi\,\Gamma(2d+1)$.
Dividing the two identities yields
\begin{equation*}
 G_d
 =\frac{2^d\Gamma(d+1)^2}{\Gamma(2d+1)}
 =\frac{2^d}{\binom{2d}{d}},
\end{equation*}
which explains the second expression in \eqref{eq:Gd-bd}.

Since $\lvert A_{\mathcal{T},d}\rvert=d\rho s^{-2}$,
the identities $\rho=(s/2)\sqrt T$ and
\eqref{eq:stereographic-T-d} give
\begin{align*}
 \int_{\mathbb{R}^d}\lvert A_{\mathcal{T},d}\rvert^d\,\mathrm{d} x
 &=d^d2^{-d}\int_{\mathbb{R}^d}s^{-d}T^{d/2}\,\mathrm{d} x=d^d2^{-2d}\int_{\mathbb{S}^d}T^{d/2}\,\mathrm{d}\omega_{\mathbb{S}^d}=d^d2^{-2d}\lvert \mathbb{S}^d\rvert G_d,
\end{align*}
which proves \eqref{eq:vector-trial-Ld-d}.

Likewise, \eqref{eq:vector-trial-pointwise-d} becomes
\[
 \lvert \nabla\wedge A_{\mathcal{T},d}\rvert^{d/2}
 =(2d)^{d/2}s^{-d}(1-T)^{d/4}.
\]
Thus \eqref{eq:stereographic-T-d} and
\eqref{eq:one-minus-T-integral-d} yield directly
\begin{align*}
 \int_{\mathbb{R}^d}\lvert \nabla\wedge A_{\mathcal{T},d}\rvert^{d/2}\,\mathrm{d} x
 &=(2d)^{d/2}2^{-d}
   \int_{\mathbb{S}^d}(1-T)^{d/4}\,\mathrm{d}\omega_{\mathbb{S}^d}=(2d)^{d/2}2^{-d}\lvert \mathbb{S}^d\rvert b_d,
\end{align*}
which proves \eqref{eq:vector-trial-energy-d}.
Dividing the two integrals and using
\eqref{eq:vector-trial-gauge-d} proves
\eqref{eq:vector-trial-powered-d}--\eqref{eq:vector-trial-unpowered-d}.

It remains to prove the strict comparison. Put $Z_d:=\Theta_d^d$. By
\eqref{eq:Gd-bd},
\begin{equation*}
 Z_d=\frac{4\binom{2d}{d}(d-1)^2}
 {(3d-2)^2[2(d-1)]^{d/2}}.
\end{equation*}
The Wallis estimate $\binom{2d}{d}<4^d/\sqrt{\pi d}$ and
$(d-1)/(3d-2)<1/3$ imply
\begin{equation*}
 Z_d<H_d:=\frac{4}{9\sqrt{\pi d}}
 \left(\frac{8}{d-1}\right)^{d/2}.
\end{equation*}
For $d\geq4$,
\begin{equation*}
 \frac{H_{d+1}}{H_d}
 =\sqrt{\frac{8}{d+1}}
   \left(1-\frac1d\right)^{d/2}
 <\sqrt{\frac{8}{e(d+1)}}<1.
\end{equation*}
Also $H_4=128/(81\sqrt\pi)<1$. Hence $Z_d<1$ for all $d\geq4$,
while direct substitution gives $Z_3=40/49<1$. This proves
\eqref{eq:Theta-d}. In odd dimensions, comparison with
\eqref{eq:LYDM-sphere} proves the strict comparison. The conclusion for
the whole family follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:vector-conformal-invariance},
homogeneity of the quotient in $A$, and gauge invariance.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
The field $A_{\mathcal{T},d}$, its exact quotient, and the strict numerical
comparison in \eqref{eq:Theta-d} are valid also for even $d$. In even
dimensions, however, there is no Loss--Yau--Dunne--Min candidate of the
form considered by Frank and Loss, so the theorem gives an explicit upper
bound for $S_d^v$ rather than the disproof of an optimizer conjecture.
Wang and Zhang had already established nonoptimality of the conformal
Loss--Yau--Dunne--Min family in every odd dimension by their spherical
second-variation argument \cite[Theorem~1.3]{WangZhangConstants}.
On the nonlinear-gauge slice
$\nabla\cdot(\lvert A\rvert^{d-2}A)=0$, their functional is related to our two
normalizations by
\[
 J_{d/2,1}(A)
 =\frac{\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^d}\lvert \nabla\wedge A\rvert^{d/2}\,\mathrm{d} x\right)^2}
        {\int_{\mathbb{R}^d}\lvert A\rvert^d\,\mathrm{d} x}
 =(R_d^v(A))^d=(\mathcal Q_d^v(A))^2.
\]
Here Lemma~\ref{lem:gauge} identifies the denominator with
$\VERT A\VERT_{d}^d$; without the nonlinear-gauge condition, this identity
need not hold. The present theorem supplies a particularly simple
explicit competitor whose quotient is evaluated in closed form.
head: environment
